en: The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Buddha Kṣīraprabha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling in Vaiśālī at the musical tree of the brahmin Mātaṅga.
Below, together with a multitude of eight hundred bhikṣus and a thousand bodhisattvas, he assembled with kings, ministers, the populace, and various devas, nāgas, and spirits to preach the sūtra.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had developed a slight case of wind-disorder and required cow’s milk.

Now, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a brahmin named Māyārī who served as the teacher of fifty thousand disciples; he was also honored and esteemed by the king, the ministers, and the common people.

He was wealthy and powerful, yet greedy and envious; he did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, took no pleasure in giving alms, and favored heterodox paths. He constantly held a net to cover his roof and courtyard so that flying birds would not invade his house to eat the grain.
The place where he resided was neither too near nor too far from the Music Garden.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Take the name of the Tathāgata and go to the house of the brahmin Māyālī; request some cow’s milk from her and bring it here."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the gate of that house.

It happened that the brahmin Māyārī was about to enter the palace with five hundred of his most eminent disciples to have an audience with the king; as he was leaving the residence, he encountered Ānanda and asked him:
"Why have you come so early this morning? What do you seek?"
Ānanda replied, "The body of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is slightly unwell; this has caused me to come early this morning to seek cow's milk.
The brahmin Māyālī remained silent and gave no answer, reflecting to himself:
"If I do not take this milk to Ānanda, people will say that I am stingy;
yet if I take this milk to him, other brahmins will again say that I serve the path of Gautama."
"Advancing or retreating, we must act with propriety.
Even so, we shall continue to direct our efforts toward the wretched cow, and have Ānanda himself milk her.

Furthermore, Gautama delights in contending with us over merit and always seeks to be the victor; we shall cause this wretched cow to gore his disciple to death. Thus, his Way will be disgraced and he will be abandoned by all, while I may once again be honored by the masses."
Whether Ānanda obtains milk or does not obtain milk, it shall simply serve to make everyone understand that I have no regard for my own life;
since the cow was killed and milk could not be obtained, my purpose has been fulfilled, and I am without fault.
After the brahmin Māyālī had deliberated on this matter, he immediately told Ānanda:
"The cow was released into that ditch this morning; you go there yourself and milk her."
Māyādevī commanded her son, saying:
"Take Ānanda to the place where these cows are; be careful not to take any cow's milk or cream yourself. Test whether Ānanda is able to obtain milk."

At that time, the five hundred disciples, having heard what their teacher said, were all greatly delighted; yet they immediately began to doubt and marvel at the matter previously mentioned by Ānanda, saying to one another:
"The ascetic Gautama always praises himself, claiming:
'I am the most honored among gods and men, and I have fully delivered all from old age, sickness, and death throughout the ten directions.'"
"For what reason and by what causes has the Buddha himself fallen ill?

After the five hundred brahmins had spoken thus together, at that time Vimalakīrti came forth, intending to go to the place where the Buddha was. On his way, he passed before the gate of the brahmin Māyālī and encountered Ānanda, whereupon he said to him:
"Why are you standing here with your alms bowl so early in the morning?"
"What do you seek?
Ānanda replied, "The Tathāgata’s body has been afflicted by a mild wind-illness and requires cow's milk; for this reason, he sent me to this place."
Vimalakīrti then said to Ānanda:
“Do not speak such words!
The body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is like a diamond; all evils have been utterly severed, and it is the convergence of all virtuous merits. How could he have any illness?”
Practice in silence; do not emulate the non-Buddhists in slandering the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, be careful not to speak again, lest the devas, nāgas, and spirits hear this sound, nor that the bodhisattvas and arhats of the ten directions all hear these words.
A Wheel-Turning Sage King, with the wheel leading the way, always attains sovereign mastery by virtue of his immeasurable merits;

how much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose body is formed through the convergence of infinite blessings from having practiced giving to all beings throughout incalculable kalpas?
Ānanda! Do not let the heterodox, those of different teachings, or the brahmins hear these words of non-conformity!
How much less can the World-Honored One, who himself has fallen ill and cannot cure it, be able to save others from old age, sickness, and death?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is the Dharma-body, not a body that has not yet attained liberation;
the Buddha is the most honored in the heavens above and the world below, he is without illness, for the Buddha’s maladies have been utterly extinguished;
the body of the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merits, and all afflictions have been eliminated.
This illness has its causes and conditions; it did not arise for no reason.
Ānanda, do not feel ashamed to seek milk.
"Walk quickly; be careful not to speak much!
Hearing this, Ānanda was filled with great shame and fear, when he heard a voice from the air saying:
"It is Ānanda!"
As the elder Vimalakīrti has said:

it is solely because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world during this degenerate age of the five turbidities that he manifests through these conditions to deliver all those in the ten directions who act with lust, anger, and delusion.
"I shall go now to fetch the milk; though Vimalakīrti spoke those words earlier, do not feel ashamed!
At that time, Ānanda was greatly astonished and marveled, thinking he must have misheard. He immediately returned to reflect, saying:
"Could this not be the result of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power moving him?"

Thereupon, when the five hundred brahmins heard what was thus spoken by the voice in the air, their minds were immediately free from doubt; they all leaped for joy and collectively resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

At that time, the brahmin Māyālī, together with his internal and external relatives and the inhabitants of the village—numbering several thousand people—all followed Ānanda to go and observe the cows.
When Ānanda arrived, he stopped beside the cows and thought to himself:
"According to the dharma of the śramaṇas for whom I serve as a teacher, one must not personally milk a cow with one's own hands."

As soon as he had finished speaking, the throne of the second Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven trembled; he then came down from heaven and, having transformed himself into the appearance of a young brahmin clad in robes, stood beside the ox.
Seeing this, Ānanda was filled with joy and said,
"Young brahmin! Please take some cow's milk."
He then replied to Ānanda:
“I am not a brahmin; I am Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the second [heaven].
Having heard that the Tathāgata desired cow’s milk, I abandoned my abode and came to this place, wishing to establish my original merit.”
Ānanda said, “The status of the Lord of Devas is so exalted; how could he draw near to such a foul and putrid ox?
Śakra replied:
"Though I am powerful, how can I compare to the Tathāgata?
Even the Honored One does not grow weary of establishing merit; how much less so a minor deity like me?
I dwell in impermanence, and all shall pass away."
"If we do not establish merit now, our store of blessings will soon be exhausted, and later we shall have nothing to rely upon.
Ānanda replied to Śakra:
"If you wish to have me take the cow's milk, I pray that you do so at once."
Śāriputra replied,
"Yes," and immediately took his bowl and went before the oxen.
At that time, the cow remained still and did not dare to move again.
Those who came to observe were all struck with wonder and said,
"What urgent business does this young brahmin have that he has come to become a disciple of Gautama and take milk from the cow?"
"If you should happen to be gored or trampled to death by this wicked bull, how could you not have let Śāntivṛtti go forward to take the cow's milk?
At that time, Śakra immediately milked the cow for Ānanda, and spoke this verse:
"Now the Buddha has a slight wind ailment; You and I shall provide him with the milk."
If one causes the Buddha to take it and cure [the ailment], the merit obtained shall be immeasurable.
The Buddha, the Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, always regards all beings with a compassionate heart;
even the smallest of crawling and flying creatures, he desires that they all be delivered and liberated.
Then the mother cow spoke this verse to Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"This hand that caresses me—how exceedingly pleasant it is!
It takes from me the milk of both udders, leaving only what remains behind."
"You should hold this for me, my son; I have not yet had a drink since morning.
Although you know that there is much merit in it, you should maintain an even mind.
Thereupon, the calf spoke a verse to his mother:
"Through countless kalpas, I have now heard the voice of the Buddha;
I declare that I shall take my own portion and offer it all to the Buddha.
The World-Honored One is the Teacher of all, and it is most difficult to behold him again."
I eat grass and drink water; this shall suffice for today.
Since I was born as a human being, I have drunk milk for a very long time;
even while among the six domestic animals, it was likewise beyond counting.
Those who are foolish in this world are also exceedingly numerous;
not knowing the Buddha’s teaching on giving, they later suffer in regret, to no avail.
In my own previous lives, I was mired in stinginess and greed, and sat idly amidst conflict.
Furthermore, following evil companions, I did not believe in the Buddha’s sutras and precepts.
This caused me to become an ox or a horse For as many as sixteen kalpas.
Now, at last, I have encountered a Buddha, Like a sick man obtaining medicine.
"Take the milk I have drunk and give it all to me, filling my bowl;
may my future wisdom allow me to attain the Way just as the Buddha has.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately took the cow’s milk for Ānanda and departed with his bowl full.
When Ānanda received the milk, his heart was filled with great joy.

At that time, the brahmins who had come from the surrounding villages to watch all heard what the mother cow and her calf had said; they were all struck with wonder and, speaking to one another, remarked:
"This cow is coarse and has always been fierce and ill-tempered; people were not permitted to approach her."
"Why are you so gentle and kind today?
I suspect this is merely the inspiration of Ānanda.
If even a disciple of Gautama can act in such a manner, how much more so must be the Buddha’s merit, majestic power, and transformations?"
"However, we did not believe in his teaching.
Immediately they were filled with joy and came to faith and understanding of the Buddha-dharma.

Māyālī the brahmin, along with the members of his household—men and women from the village numbering more than ten thousand—all leaped for joy; they distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the Dharma-eye.
Ānanda took the milk and returned to where the Buddha was. At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to several thousand people.
Ānanda immediately stepped forward, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just now, while I was sent on an errand to the house of the brahmin Māyālī to seek milk, the mother and calf of the cow spoke in human speech."
When I heard their words, I was greatly astonished and marveled at them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“What did this mother cow and her calf say that you find so doubtful?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"This Māyā has an ox that is extremely vicious and fond of goring and trampling people.
No one in the household dares to approach it."
Although the owner does not milk the cow, she merely causes it to produce milk.
This cow naturally gives birth to a calf that is large and excellent, surpassing all other calves by a hundred thousandfold.
The brahmin secretly instructed his son, forbidding him from allowing me to take the milk.
I thought to myself:
"According to the dharma of a śramaṇa, one should not take things with one's own hands."

As soon as these words were finished, the second Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately arrived and descended, transforming himself into the appearance of a young Brahmin clad in robes, and stood beside the cow.
I said to him:
"I beg you to milk this cow for me."
Śakra replied, "So be it.
He then stepped forward to take the milk and addressed the cow, saying:
"Now the World-Honored One has a slight wind ailment and requires milk.
If you provide milk to the Tathāgata, you shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Thereupon, the cow replied to Śakra:
"Take my two udders and set aside the milk from both to give to my calf.
While the calf was by its mother's side, it heard the name of the World-Honored One and its heart was filled with great joy;
it then said to its mother, "Give all my share of milk to the Buddha."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the teacher of gods and humans, is extremely difficult to encounter.
When I was a human, I drank milk for a very long time; when I was an animal, it was likewise so.
The world is filled with great ignorance; most do not know that by practicing giving, one shall obtain blessings in future lives.
In my previous existence, I followed evil friends, did not believe in the Way of the Sutras, and took pleasure in being contentious and aggressive.
For this reason, I fell among cattle and horses for sixteen kalpas before finally being able to hear the voice of a Buddha.
Taking all the remaining milk, I offered it to the Tathāgata, vowing that in the future my wisdom might attain the Way as he has.
"Thus did the mother cow and her calf speak of this matter.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"It is exactly as the mother cow and her calf have said."
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively to what I shall say.

This mother cow and her calf were, in a former life, once a householder who was immensely wealthy and prosperous, possessing abundant riches and treasures. Yet, they were stingy and greedy, unwilling to practice charity; they did not believe in the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, nor did they understand the root of birth and death."
He always delighted in lending money; when outsiders came to borrow at interest, as the days and months arrived, he took pleasure in the accumulation of large debts and interest.
Lacking any sense of propriety, once the principal had been repaid, he would further deceive and defraud others, claiming that the payment was not yet complete.
"However, because of this very act, you fell among the animals for sixteen kalpas.
Why is it that upon hearing my name, you feel such joy?
The retribution for your animal offenses shall now come to an end; therefore, upon hearing the Buddha's voice, you immediately conceived a heart of compassion and gave milk to the Buddha."
"By means of these causes and conditions, you shall attain liberation.

At that time, the Buddha smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth. Heaven and earth shook violently, and the light illuminated the ten directions; it then circled his body three times and divided into two parts:
one part entered through his navel, and the other part entered through the crown of his head, whereupon they vanished.
Thereupon Ānanda immediately stepped forward, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must surely be a reason for this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What you have asked is most excellent! Why is this?

After the lives of this mother and her calf come to an end, they will be reborn seven times in the Tuṣita Heaven and the Brahma Heavens, and seven times in the human world, where they shall become sons of wealthy and noble families, never again being born into the three evil realms."

Wherever you may be, you should always possess the knowledge of past lives; you should make offerings to the Buddhas by hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies, scattering flowers and burning incense, and receiving and upholding the teachings of the sutras.

Due to these causes and conditions, the mother cow shall, in her final existence, encounter Maitreya Buddha; she will become a śramaṇa and, through diligent practice for no long time, shall attain the path of arhatship.
The calf shall likewise do so; after twenty kalpas have passed, he shall become a buddha named Kṣīraprabha (Light of Milk), and his land shall be named Dhvajaprabhāsa (Radiance of Banners).

When the Tathāgata Kṣīraprabha attains Buddhahood, he shall deliver the myriad people of the heavens and the world, as well as all classes of crawling and flying creatures, in numbers equal to the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, the people of the country all lived for seven thousand years; their clothing and food were like those of the Uttarakuru Heaven in the northern quarter.
The Buddha remained in the world teaching for forty thousand years, and after his parinirvāṇa, the sutras and Dharma remained for ten thousand years before finally coming to an end.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The mother and calf, with a sincere heart and virtuous intention, gave milk to the Tathāgata; both shall attain liberation.”
If even animals still possess a virtuous mind, how much more so should those who have become human?

With their six sense faculties complete, they are able to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly; yet they do not believe in where birth originates from or where death leads to, nor do they understand the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, nor do they believe that giving alms will result in receiving blessings in future lives.
It is solely because people sit bound by stinginess and greed that they deceive themselves; their minds harbor evil thoughts, their mouths utter evil words, and their bodies commit evil deeds.
It is through these very things that foolish people fail to attain liberation.
When the sutra had been preached, five hundred sons of elders within the assembly all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Three thousand eight hundred brahmins, who originally did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, leaped for joy and rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Five hundred others, who originally did not believe in the cycle of birth and death or in sin and merit, beheld the Buddha’s miraculous transformations and all received the five precepts to become lay devotees (*upāsakas*).
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus, elders, brahmins, and the common people were all greatly rejoiced; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Buddha Kṣīraprabha (The Buddha-Spoken Scripture of the Buddha Milk-Light)
